draft.title: Lake Mungo
card: Lake Mungo is in the Willandra Lakes region of western New South Wales. The lakes are now dry, but long ago they held water and supported people.
Remains found there are about 40,000 years old. They include a woman who was cremated and a man who was buried.
Burial and cremation are rites: set ways of treating the dead. They show that people cared for their dead and had shared beliefs.
These are among the oldest known burial and cremation rites in the world. Mungo is part of the Willandra Lakes Region World Heritage Area.
draft.remember: Mungo's 40,000-year-old remains show early rites for the dead, among the oldest known.

a.q: What do the burial and cremation remains at Lake Mungo tell historians?
opts: Early people had rites for the dead and shared beliefs
Early people lived only beside lakes that never dried
Early people had no ways of caring for each other
Early people arrived in Australia only 40,000 years ago
a.why: Treating the dead in set ways shows care and shared beliefs. The remains are about 40,000 years old, but that does not mean people arrived then, because the card gives only the age of these remains.
a.clue: Think about what a rite for the dead shows about the living.

opts: They show rites for the dead from about 40,000 years ago
They show where the lakes of western New South Wales are

They show that people only began to bury the dead at Mungo
b.why: The remains are about 40,000 years old and show early rites for the dead, which is why they are so important. The lakes are now dry, but the remains do not show they were always dry. The card also says they are among the oldest known, not the first anywhere.
b.clue: Look for the option about age and rites, not about the lakes.

proposal.title: Lake Mungo
card: Lake Mungo is in the Willandra Lakes region of western New South Wales. The lakes are now dry, but long ago they held water and supported people.
Remains found there are about 40,000 years old. They include a woman who was cremated and a man who was buried, now known as Mungo Lady and Mungo Man. Both have since been returned to Country.
Burial and cremation are both rites: set ways of treating the dead. They show that people cared for their dead and had shared beliefs.
These are among the oldest known burial and cremation rites in the world. People were living in Australia well before this time.
proposal.remember: About 40,000 years ago, people at Mungo cared for their dead through set rites, among the oldest known.

a.q: What do the burial and cremation remains at Lake Mungo tell historians?
opts: People there had shared beliefs about the dead
People there first reached Australia at that time
People there cremated their dead but did not bury them
People there left their dead where they had died
a.why: Treating the dead in set ways shows care and shared beliefs. The remains are about 40,000 years old, but people were living in Australia well before this, so they do not mark the first arrivals.
a.clue: Think about what a rite for the dead shows about the living.

b.q: At Mungo, a woman was cremated and a man was buried, both about 40,000 years ago. What does this suggest?
opts: People had more than one rite for treating the dead
One of the two was cared for and the other was not
The buried man lived many thousands of years later
Burial was a rite there but cremation was not
b.why: Burial and cremation are both set ways of treating the dead, so people at Mungo had more than one rite. It is tempting to think only one was cared for, but both rites show care for the dead.
